# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-20 (Extended v148)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826; **current narrative point (winter Year 5, early morning—4 a.m. and dawn following escape night)**: Paris—Rue Plumet (Valjean's primary house); Rue de Babylone (secret passage exit); Luxembourg; Salpêtrière district; garden near Austerlitz settlement; Place de la Bastille (elephant monument under construction); Impasse de la Planchette (blind alley); Orme-Saint-Gervais district; Prison Charlemagne (New Building and Fine-Air top story); Rue des Ballets; Rue du Roi-de-Sicile; Rue Saint-Antoine; ruin wall of La Force; Ravenmere and other English provincial towns (Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Wilwick, Salcombe, Dunstead, Staveford). **Seasonal progression**: Winter Year 5 environment (wintry gale, rain with thunder, showers, frost silvering hedges, muddy roads with ruts and puddles after thaw, smoke lying flat over fields, salt and tar harbor smell, children chasing hoops, bees in lavender, vespers bells, bakery lines, market-gardeners' descent from Montreuil/Charonne/Vincennes/Bercy through Rue Saint-Antoine, early darkness).

## Primary Locations
**RUE PLUMET HOUSE**: Single-story pavilion in deserted Rue Plumet with garden approximately one-and-a-half acres. Two ground-floor rooms, two first-floor chambers, downstairs kitchen, upstairs boudoir, attic. Behind pavilion: narrow courtyard, low building (two rooms, cellar). Secret-spring door masked in building communicates via long narrow paved winding corridor to Rue de Babylone quarter-league distant. Garden characteristics: Left uncultivated; breathes melancholy, solitude, liberty, absence of man, presence of God.

**PLACE DE LA BASTILLE & ELEPHANT MONUMENT**: Rough model, marvelous sketch of Napoleon's idea. Elephant forty feet high, constructed of timber and masonry, bearing tower resembling house, formerly painted green, now black. Broad brow, trunk, tusks, tower, crupper, four feet like columns. In 1832: enveloped in immense shirt of woodwork, surrounded by vast plank enclosure. Gap in fence provides entry; timber-yard nearby with ladder for laborers.

**ELEPHANT'S INTERIOR (GAVROCHE'S REFUGE)**: Interior accessed via black hole in belly near foreleg. Vast hollow space. Long brown beam forming vertebral column with massive arching ribs. Stalactites of plaster; vast spiders' webs. **Rats swarming by thousands—frightened by voices but return when silent.** Three long poles thrust into floor rubbish, consolidated at summits with rope forming pyramidal bundle. Trellis-work of brass wire enveloping poles, held by iron wire fastenings. Row of heavy stones keeping network down to floor. Grating creates cage-like enclosure. Gavroche's bed situated behind net. **Large crack in roof where flue enters—easy access point.**

**PRISON CHARLEMAGNE (NEW BUILDING & FINE-AIR)**: Ancient decrepit structure. Contains four dormitories, one above another, plus top story called "Bel-Air" (Fine-Air). Large chimney-flue from ancient kitchen of Dukes de la Force starts ground floor, traverses all four stories, cuts dormitories as flattened pillar, pierces roof. Roofers currently re-laying slates on prison, creating scaffoldings and ladders. Fine-Air: Large hall with Mansard roof, guarded with triple gratings and double doors of sheet iron. Four dormer-windows at north end. Four square cages separated by narrow passages, built of masonry to elbow height, rest to roof of iron bars. Lighted by skylight. Sentry relieved every two hours, marches with loaded musket. Jailer escorted by two dogs enters daily at four o'clock, deposits loaf of black bread, jug of water, bowl of thin bouillon, inspects irons. Two visits during night. Prisoners wear fetters weighing fifty pounds.

**RUE DES BALLETS/RUE DU ROI-DE-SICILE RUIN**: Back wall of masonry rising to height of third story. Two large square windows; middle one barred with worm-eaten beam. Wall fragment of outer wall of La Force. Empty space half-filled by fence of rotten boards shored by five stone posts. Recess conceals little shanty leaning against ruin remnant. Fence has gate fastened only by latch. **Steep escarpment three stories high separates ruin edge from pavement of street below.**

## Jean Valjean's Recovery and Mysterious Activity (October 1831—Winter Year 5)
**The wound and illness**: Day following Jondrette visit, Valjean appeared with large inflamed wound on left arm resembling burn (origin unclear). Detained in house one month with fever; refused doctor. Cosette deserted pavilion, devoted herself entirely to his care.

**March-April transformation**: Valjean convalesced; happiness reviving in ineffable rays; clouds upon his soul growing dim.

**Charitable activities resumed**: Carry bread to hungry, clothing to cold. Cosette often accompanied Valjean on visits to poor.

**Mysterious journeys**: Valjean took occasional journeys at long intervals, absent one or two days utmost. Destination unknown, even to Cosette. Pattern: journeys typically when money lacking in house.

**Nocturnal garden activity and manuscript delivery**: Cosette observed figure walking beneath trees in garden dusk, carrying large club. Found stone on garden bench; became alarmed, fled, closed shutters. Later discovered packet of leaflets on garden bench—manuscript containing extended philosophical meditation on love as divine spark—immortal, incorruptible, infinite, burning to marrow of bones, beaming in depths of heaven.

## Marius and Cosette's Romance
**Cosette's recognition and revelation (autumn Year 5)**: Upon reading manuscript, recognized writer as Marius. Acknowledged she had never truly forgotten him, had always loved and adored him. "The fire had been smothered, and had smouldered for a time," but now "it had burst forth afresh, and had inflamed her whole being."

**Garden encounter (autumn Year 5)**: Marius grasped Cosette in garden as she fell. He took her in arms, pressed her close, "without knowing what he was doing." Supported her though tottering himself. They fell upon bench. Their lips met without knowing how. Night serene and splendid overhead. "Effusion followed silence, which is fulness." Two beings "pure as spirits" told each other everything—dreams, intoxications, ecstasies, chimæras, weaknesses. Confided how they had adored each other from afar, longed, despaired. "Their two hearts poured themselves out into each other in such wise, that at the expiration of a quarter of an hour, it was the young man who had the young girl's soul, and the young girl who had the young man's soul. Each became permeated with the other, they were enchanted with each other, they dazzled each other."

## Thénardiers and Child Substitution
**Family disruption**: Thénardiers in prison following Jondrette garret arrest.

**Magnon arrangement**: Before police raid, Thénardier handed two little sons to Magnon (fashionable woman in criminal sphere) with express intention of renouncing them forever. Magnon promised ten francs monthly, actually paid. M. Gillenormand (grandfather) continued compact—came every six months to see children, did not perceive change. Children well cared for, well clothed, adequately fed, treated almost like little gentlemen—better by false mother than real mother.

**Spring 1832 dispersal**: Shortly after Magnon handed note to Éponine, sudden police raid made in Rue Clocheperce. Magnon and Mamselle Miss (clever gallicized English thief, naturalized Parisienne, intimately connected with medals and diamonds) seized; house emptied. **Spring 1832: The two children set out alone**. Elder leading younger, holding paper with address **M. Barge, collector of rents, Rue du Roi-de-Sicile, No. 8**. At corner of Rue Clocheperce, gust of wind tore paper from elder's benumbed fingers; as night falling, child unable to find it again. **Lost in city, wandering in spring cold.**

## Gavroche and the Two Lost Children
**Gavroche's character and activities**: Street child, homeless, hungry, clever pickpocket. Stole Montparnasse's purse (late April Year 5). "Always shivering gayly under his rags." Wears woman's woollen shawl converted into neck comforter. Engages in "shaving barbers"—stealing cakes of soap from shop-fronts to sell for sou to hair-dressers in suburbs.

**Encounter with two lost children (spring 1832)**: While scrutinizing wig-maker's shop window near Orme-Saint-Gervais, observed two children of unequal stature, very neatly dressed. Barber thrust them back furiously, slammed door. Gavroche provided bread and promised shelter.

**Rescue and shelter (spring-to-winter Year 5)**: Led two children through gap in fence into elephant's enclosure at Place de la Bastille. Raised ladder from timber-yard. Climbed to black hole in elephant's belly. Elder child undertook risk of climbing; younger felt greatly inclined to cry but did not dare. Gavroche descended, grasped child of five, planted him on ladder, climbed behind him. All three sheltered inside elephant through winter Year 5.

**Winter Year 5 nocturnal incident**: Five-year-old boy heard hubbub overhead (possibly rat attack during darkness), jogged elder brother's elbow. Elder had already shut eyes as Gavroche ordered. Younger brother questioned Gavroche in low tone. **Gavroche grasped little fellow's hand across his brother; child felt reassured.** Courage and strength communicated mysteriously. Silence reigned; sound of voices frightened rats off. Within few minutes rats returned. **All three fell fast asleep during wintry gale and rain.** Monster sheltered from heaven and men the three poor sleeping children.

## Prison Escape: Brujon, Guelemer, Babet, Montparnasse, and Thénardier (Winter Year 5, Early Morning—4 a.m. and Dawn)
**Brujon's background**: Dangerous prisoner with appearance of delicate health and profoundly premeditated languor. Polished, intelligent sprig and thief. First studies in art directed to roofs. Made great progress in "double pickings"—tearing off lead, plundering roofs, despoiling gutters.

**Thénardier's confinement**: **Rated as burglar, detained as measure of precaution under charge of organizing nocturnal ambush with armed force, kept in sight in one of four cages in Fine-Air since night of 3d of February.** Kept on feet fetters weighing fifty pounds. Obtained permission to keep iron bolt to spike bread into wall crack "to preserve it from rats." Procured and secreted bottle of wine with narcotic invented by Desrues, rendered famous by band of _Endormeurs_ (Sleep-compellers). Sentry relieved every two hours marched in front of cage with loaded musket.

**Night of escape—Brujon and Guelemer**: **When Gavroche picked up two lost children, Brujon and Guelemer, who knew Babet had escaped that morning and waited in street along with Montparnasse, rose softly and with nail Brujon had found, began to pierce chimney against which their beds stood.** Rubbish fell on Brujon's bed, unheard. Showers mingled with thunder created terrible and opportune uproar. Prisoners who woke pretended to fall asleep, left Guelemer and Brujon to devices. Before sound reached watcher, wall pierced, chimney scaled, iron grating barred upper orifice of flue forced, two redoubtable ruffians on roof. Wind and rain redoubled, roof slippery. Abyss six feet broad and eighty feet deep separated them from surrounding wall. Fastened rope Brujon spun in dungeon to stumps of iron bars just wrenched off, flung other over outer wall, crossed abyss at one bound, clung to coping of wall, got astride of it, let themselves slip along rope upon little roof touching bath-house, pulled rope after them, jumped down into courtyard of bath-house, traversed it, pushed open porter's wicket, pulled rope, opened porte-cochère, found themselves in street. **Successfully escaped.**

**Thénardier's escape—night to early morning**: At two o'clock in morning, old soldier sentinel relieved and replaced by conscript. Few moments later, man with dogs paid visit, went off without noticing except possibly excessive youth and "rustic air" of "raw recruit." Two hours afterwards, at four o'clock, when came to relieve conscript, he was found asleep on floor lying like log near Thénardier's cage. **Thénardier no longer there. Hole in ceiling of cage and above it hole in roof. One plank of bed wrenched off, probably carried away.** Half-empty bottle containing remains of stupefying wine seized in cell. **Soldier's bayonet disappeared.** At all events, **Thénardier dripping with perspiration, drenched with rain, clothes hanging in ribbons, hands flayed, elbows bleeding, knees torn, had reached edge of wall of ruin at Rue des Ballets/Rue du Roi-de-Sicile; there stretched himself out at full length; there his strength had failed him. Steep escarpment three stories high separated him from pavement of street.**

**Four o'clock and dawn—discovery and pursuit**: Four o'clock struck. Thénardier shuddered. Terrified and confused uproar broke forth in prison. Sound of doors opening and shutting, creaking of gratings, tumult in guard-house, hoarse shouts of turnkeys, shock of musket-butts on pavement, reached his ears. Lights ascended and descended past grated windows of dormitories, torch ran along ridge-pole of top story of New Building, firemen belonging in barracks on right summoned. Their helmets, lighted up in rain, went and came along roofs. **At same time, Thénardier perceived in direction of Bastille a wan whiteness lighting up edge of sky in doleful wise—dawn arriving.**

**Thénardier on wall waiting for rescue**: **Thénardier waited, pale, exhausted, desperate with all despair he had undergone, still hidden by night but telling himself day was on point of dawning, alarmed at idea of hearing neighboring clock of Saint-Paul strike four within few minutes, hour when sentinel relieved and latter would be found asleep under pierced roof.** Staring in horror at terrible depth, at light of street lanterns, wet black pavement—pavement longed for yet frightful, which meant death and which meant liberty. Asked himself whether his three accomplices in flight had succeeded, if they had heard him, if they would come to his assistance. Listened. With exception of patrol, no one had passed through street since he had been there.

**Four ruffians' rescue attempt and retreat**: **Brujon and Guelemer, along with Babet and Montparnasse, had prowled all night long about La Force in hope of seeing Thénardier make his appearance on top of some wall.** Night growing too fine—downpour rendered all streets deserted—cold overpowering them, soaked garments, hole-ridden shoes, alarming noise burst forth in prison, hours elapsed, patrol encountered, hope vanishing, all urged them to beat retreat. **Montparnasse himself, perhaps almost Thénardier's son-in-law, yielded.** Moment more and they would be gone. **Thénardier was panting on his wall like shipwrecked sufferers of _Méduse_ on their raft when they beheld vessel which had appeared in sight vanish on horizon.**

**Guelemer and Gavroche's connection**: **Guelemer seized Gavroche by one arm, set him on roof of shanty (whose worm-eaten planks bent beneath urchin's weight), and handed him rope which Brujon had knotted together during Montparnasse's absence.** **Gavroche directed his steps towards flue—easy to enter thanks to large crack touching roof.** **At moment when on point of ascending, Thénardier saw life and safety approaching, bent over edge of wall; first light of dawn struck white upon his brow dripping with sweat, upon his livid cheek-bones, sharp and savage nose, bristling gray beard, and Gavroche recognized him.**

**Gavroche's condition after escape**: As soon as Gavroche touched pavement, as soon as he found himself out of danger, he was no longer either weary, chilled or trembling; terrible things from which he had escaped vanished like smoke, strange and ferocious mind awoke once more, stood erect and free, ready to march onward.

## Authorial Digression on Argot
**Narrative voice**: Narrator defends representation of criminal language (argot) as legitimate literary subject. Four and thirty years ago, when narrator introduced thief who talked argot, arose amazement and clamor. Claims two powerful romancers—Balzac and Eugène Sue (described as profound observer of human heart and intrepid friend of the people)—have since represented ruffians as talking natural language, as author of _The Last Day of a Condemned Man_ did in 1828, same objections raised. Narrator argues: "Why should one not explore everything, and study everything? Why should one halt on the way? The halt is a matter depending on the sounding-line, and not on the leadsman." Questions when it became wrong to probe wound, gulf, society—to go to bottom.

## Supporting Characters and Provincial Elements
**Father Mabeuf**: Old man in Austerlitz settlement garden; capable of extraordinary physical prowess despite age; defeated Montparnasse in unexpected reversal (late April Year 5).

**Montparnasse**: Elegant ruffian, eighteen years old; rose in mouth; well-dressed in fine black coat; unexpectedly defeated by Father Mabeuf; thief victim of Gavroche; warned Gavroche of police. **Participated in all-night vigil around La Force early morning winter Year 5; yielded to retreat with other ruffians.**

**Lieutenant Théodule**: Handsome officer of lancers, apparently eighteen or younger; vain, insolent; passed Rue Plumet gate autumn Year 5; smiled at Cosette (she found him insipid, silly, stupid, useless, foppish, displeasing, impertinent, extremely ugly).

**Toussaint**: House servant; fastens shutters; terrifies Cosette with melodrama about assassins.

**Marius**: Young stranger from Luxembourg; author of philosophical manuscript on divine love; present in garden autumn Year 5 for encounter with Cosette; recognized her from Luxembourg meetings.

**Magnon's associate**: Mamselle Miss—clever gallicized English thief, naturalized Parisienne, seized in Rue Clocheperce police raid.

**Babet and Brujon**: Criminal associates; Babet escaped morning of prison escape night; Brujon successfully escaped via chimney and roof with Guelemer. **Both participated in all-night vigil around La Force with Montparnasse and Guelemer.**

**Provincial figures (background detail)**: Semor Brackick in Ravenmere; Tatho Brackick moved to Salcombe; Kassa mended torn sleeve by window.

## Key States (Winter Year 5, Early Morning—4 a.m. and Dawn)
- **Cosette's emotional state** (autumn through winter Year 5): Transformed from confusion and terror to luminous joy upon discovering Marius's manuscript. Fire of love reignited. Exchanged intimate conversation with Marius; hearts poured into each other; became permeated with each other, enchanted, dazzled.
- **Two lost Thénardier children and Gavroche** (spring 1832 through winter Year 5): **Still sheltered inside Place de la Bastille elephant monument, winter Year 5 early morning. Five-year-old terrified by hubbub (possibly rats), reassured by Gavroche's hand-grasp. All three fell fast asleep during wintry gale and rain.** Gavroche directed toward elephant flue by Guelemer with rope.
- **Thénardier** (winter Year 5, 4 a.m. to dawn): **Escaped from Fine-Air cage early morning winter Year 5. Reached edge of wall of ruin at Rue des Ballets/Rue du Roi-de-Sicile; strength failed him. Separated from street pavement below by steep three-story escarpment. Waited in desperation expecting rescue as four ruffians (Brujon, Guelemer, Babet, Montparnasse) prowled all night. Ruffians retreated at dawn as hope vanished. Status: escaped prisoner on ruin edge, desperate, unable to descend, awaiting potential rescue.**
- **Brujon, Guelemer, Babet, Montparnasse**: **Successfully escaped from Prison Charlemagne via roof, chimney, rope across abyss, bath-house courtyard, escaped into street winter Year 5 early morning. Spent all-night vigil around La Force for Thénardier; retreated at dawn when hope vanished.**
- **Season/Time**: Winter Year 5, early morning—approximately 4 a.m. transitioning to dawn. Four o'clock clock-strike; wintry gale with rain, thunder, frost, muddy roads, smoke lying flat, salt and tar harbor smell; bakery activity, children with hoops, bees in lavender.
